annotations.text:
H3 · Full width, at rest — the third cut, and the one that actually resolves the squeeze.

The lane rail stays, because 132px buys meaning. The inspector does not, because it only earns its 320-400px while you are reading one step. So at rest the canvas gets 1275px: six columns, nine steps, no run strip, no edge fade, nothing cut off. The whole run is one glance.

That is the right trade for the primary task. Triage is scanning — you want the shape and the three trouble spots at once — and this is the only layout that gives you all of it, including the fan back out of the human lane into two parallel provisioning steps.

H3 · The same canvas, inspecting.

The drawer overlays rather than taking a column, so the graph does not reflow — nothing you were looking at moves under you. It is the app's own glass at a higher opacity, which means the two queued steps it covers still read underneath instead of vanishing, and a tail on its left edge points at the node it belongs to. The selected step wears a heavier halo than its resting review ring.

Tradeoff: it does cover the right third while open, so a node selected far right needs the canvas to pan to it. Worth it — that is a focused task, and closing the drawer is one click back to the full run.

H1 · Horizontal console — the first cut. A's chrome turned on its side, both side panels kept.

Four columns of node fit at 1440, so the run strip along the bottom carries all eleven steps in order and colour, with the accent window showing what the canvas is looking at.

Tradeoff: 148px nodes, two-line titles, one detail line. Superseded by H3 above unless you want the tenant rail permanently visible.

H2 · Lanes — where the lane idea came from. The left column stops being navigation and starts being meaning: agent on top, external systems in the middle, human review at the bottom.

H3 above keeps this rail and spends the reclaimed inspector column on the graph instead.

Direction A · Console — the vertical original.

Why: the tenant, the flow and the run all stay on screen, so switching runs is one click and the triage strip answers "is anything broken" before you look at the graph. The inspector has real room for a payload, a retry history and the tool calls.

Tradeoff: the most chrome of the three. At 1280 and below the rail has to collapse and the inspector has to become an overlay, or the canvas gets squeezed to nothing.

The same console holding a 5-step linear run — and the reason waiting is not a colour.

Nothing here failed. The step is polling an ACH processor with two retries left, so it gets a dashed border, a clock and two secondary buttons. Compare the inspector to the one on the left: no accent anywhere, because nobody has to do anything yet.

Direction B · Spotlight.

Why: no chrome at all. Everything that has settled dims to 45%, so what is left at full strength IS the answer — the failed step and the one holding for you. The header, triage and inspector float as glass over the canvas, which is the demo's own visual language taken to its end.

Tradeoff: the floating inspector covers graph you might want to see, and there is nowhere to switch tenants or runs without leaving the view.

Direction C · Trace + shape.

Why: it reuses the chat's turn trace verbatim. The left column is the run as a story — rail alongside what ran, frayed where the sanctions call died, then back out flush for the sentence that speaks to you. The graph on the right carries shape only, so it never has to hold detail.

Tradeoff: two representations of one run means two things to keep in sync, and the trace column degrades on a wide fan-out where order stops meaning much.

The vocabulary all the directions share, plus what the Nunito swap actually costs.

Every value on this sheet already exists as a token in brand.css. The flow viewer adds no new colours — the one new idea is that a node which needs a human is the only node that carries a button.
